title: System Design Concepts Course and Interview Prep
description: A structured path through freeCodeCamp’s system design interview-prep video with Hayk Simonyan. Watch each chapter in the original YouTube video, then use the summary, quiz, and exercise to lock in the idea. The course surveys the core building blocks of scalable systems: architecture, CAP and service objectives, networking, APIs, caching, proxies, load balancing, and databases.

source.name: freeCodeCamp.org

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.summary: Hayk Simonyan frames this as a crash course on the system design interview concepts you need, covering scalability, reliability, data handling, and high-level architecture. He stresses that the interview is not mainly about writing code; interviewers want to see how you glue an entire large-scale system together.

quiz.question: What is a system design interview mainly trying to assess, according to this course’s framing?
choices: How quickly you can write production-ready code on a whiteboard
How you connect the parts of a large system, not how you write the implementation code
Whether you can memorize every AWS product name
How many sorting algorithms you can implement
quiz.explanation: The course describes the interview as being about gluing an entire system together rather than writing actual code.

quiz.question: Which trio does the course treat as central activities in system design?
choices: Compiling, linking, and deploying
Moving data, storing data, and transforming data
Marketing, billing, and support
Linting, formatting, and testing
quiz.explanation: Those three activities are the high-level lens used at the start of the course.

exercise.prompt: In two or three sentences, describe a product you know (for example a chat app or a shop) in terms of how it moves, stores, and transforms data.
exercise.hint: Moving might be a user request or a message between services; storing might be a database or object store; transforming might be creating a feed, a receipt, or an analytics aggregate.

lessons.content:
## What this crash course is for

This is a complete crash course on the system design concepts you need for a job interview, taught by Hayk Simonyan. The tutorial promises clear explanations, real-world examples, and practical strategies covering scalability, reliability, data handling, and high-level architecture.

Hayk starts with a point that shapes how you should study the rest of the course: a system design interview is not primarily a coding interview. Interviewers generally do not want to watch you write implementation code. They want to see how you *glue an entire system together* — how the pieces connect, what you would put where, and why.

## What “gluing a system together” means

In this kind of interview you are asked to design something large: a feed, a store, a chat service, a video platform. The work is to choose components, describe how data moves, and talk through trade-offs. You still need technical knowledge — networks, APIs, caches, databases — but you use that knowledge to explain a shape, not to implement a class.

That is why this course walks through core concepts before it asks you to design a full system. If you do not know what a load balancer or a cache is for, you cannot honestly place one on a diagram or defend the choice.

The intro is short on purpose. It is a frame for everything that follows: treat each later lesson as a building block you will later assemble, and keep the interview goal in mind — show that you can think at the level of a whole system, not only a single function.

## Common pitfalls

- Walking into a system design interview ready to write code, and under-preparing the “how does this all fit?” story.
- Memorizing component names without being able to say what problem each one solves.
- Skipping the fundamentals and jumping straight to a fashionable architecture that you cannot justify.

## Key takeaways

- This course is a crash course in system design interview concepts: scalability, reliability, data, and high-level architecture.
- The interview is about assembling a system, not about writing production code on a whiteboard.
- Later lessons give you the vocabulary and trade-offs you need to do that assembly honestly.

lessons.title: Computer architecture

chapters.title: Computer Architecture (Disk Storage, RAM, Cache, CPU)

lessons.summary: Before designing distributed systems, the course reviews how a single computer actually runs code. Computers work in layers and, at the core, only understand binary bits. The lesson then walks the storage and compute hierarchy — disk, RAM, cache, and the CPU — so you have intuition for why some operations are cheap, why memory is scarce, and why caches exist.

quiz.question: In the usual storage hierarchy, which of these is typically the fastest but smallest?
choices: Hard disk or SSD storage
RAM
CPU cache
Magnetic tape backup
quiz.explanation: Cache sits closest to the CPU: it is small and expensive, but much faster than RAM or disk.

quiz.question: Why does this hardware review matter in a system design interview?
choices: Interviewers only hire people who can solder RAM
It explains why some operations are cheap or slow, and why we cache data closer to the processor or the user
It replaces the need to talk about databases
It proves that disk is always faster than memory
quiz.explanation: The point is performance intuition, not hardware assembly.

exercise.prompt: Order disk, RAM, and CPU cache from fastest to slowest, and write one sentence about why an application might keep a frequently used value in memory instead of reading it from disk every time.
exercise.hint: Fastest is cache, then RAM, then disk. Re-reading from disk on every request adds latency.

lessons.content:
## Start with one machine

Before you design a large distributed system, it helps to know how a single computer actually runs your code. Hayk walks through the machine as a set of layers, each optimized for a different job, all the way from bits up to the CPU and the motherboard that connects them.

At the bottom, computers only understand binary: zeros and ones. A bit is the smallest unit and is either 0 or 1. A byte is eight bits and can represent a character such as “a” or a small number. From there we name larger amounts of storage: kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes, and terabytes.

## Storage: disk, RAM, and cache

**Disk** is the computer’s long-term storage. It can be a hard disk drive (HDD) or a solid-state drive (SSD). Disk is *non-volatile*: if you turn the machine off, the data is still there. It holds the operating system, applications, and user files. Typical sizes run from hundreds of gigabytes to multiple terabytes. SSDs cost more than HDDs but are much faster. Hayk gives example read speeds of about 500–3,500 MB/s for an SSD versus about 80–160 MB/s for an HDD.

**RAM** (random access memory) is the next place data lives when a program is actually running. It holds data structures, variables, intermediate computations, and the runtime stack — the working set of the program. RAM is *volatile*: it needs power, and its contents are gone after a restart. Consumer machines may have a few gigabytes; high-end servers can have hundreds. Read and write speeds often exceed 5,000 MB/s, faster than even a fast SSD.

Sometimes even RAM is not fast enough, which is why we have **cache**. CPU cache is smaller than RAM, typically measured in megabytes, but access is much faster — on the order of a few nanoseconds for L1. When the CPU needs data, it checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, and only then RAM. The point of the cache is to reduce the average time to get data, by keeping frequently used values close to the processor.

```text
CPU  →  L1 cache  →  L2/L3 cache  →  RAM  →  Disk (SSD/HDD)
fast, small                         slower, larger, durable
```

## CPU, compilation, and the motherboard

The **CPU** is the brain of the computer. It fetches, decodes, and executes instructions. When you run a program, it is the CPU that performs the operations.

Code you write in a high-level language such as Java, C++, or Python cannot be executed as-is. A compiler (or a related translation step) turns it into machine code the CPU can run. Once it is in that form, the CPU can read and write RAM, disk, and cache as the program requires.

The **motherboard** (or main board) is the component that connects everything. It provides the pathways that let data move among CPU, memory, and storage.

These speed and volatility differences show up again when you design systems: a cache in front of a database is the same idea as L1 in front of RAM, just at a different scale.

## Common pitfalls

- Treating disk and RAM as interchangeable. Disk survives a reboot; RAM does not.
- Assuming a bigger disk automatically makes a program faster. If the working set is in RAM or cache, disk speed may barely matter.
- Forgetting the cache hierarchy and thinking every memory access costs the same.

## Key takeaways

- Data lives in a hierarchy: bits and bytes on disk, working data in RAM, the hottest data in CPU cache.
- Disk is non-volatile; RAM and typically cache are volatile.
- SSDs are faster and more expensive than HDDs; RAM is faster still; L1 cache is fastest and smallest.
- The CPU executes machine code; a compiler translates high-level languages into that form.
- The motherboard is the interconnect among these parts.

lessons.title: Production app architecture

chapters.title: Production App Architecture (CI/CD, Load Balancers, Logging & Monitoring)

lessons.summary: A production app is more than one process on a laptop. Hayk starts with a CI/CD pipeline (continuous integration and continuous deployment) so code can go from a repository through tests and onto production without manual steps, using tools such as Jenkins or GitHub Actions. He then places load balancers in front of the app and adds logging and monitoring so you can see what the system is doing once it is live.

quiz.question: Which CI/CD tools does this lesson mention as examples for automating deployment?
choices: Jenkins or GitHub Actions
Only Photoshop
Only FTP clients
Excel macros
quiz.explanation: Hayk names platforms such as Jenkins or GitHub Actions for automating the path from the repository through tests to production.

quiz.question: Besides a CI/CD pipeline, which supporting pieces appear in this high-level production architecture?
choices: Load balancers plus logging and monitoring
Only a single laptop process with no tests
A paper filing cabinet
A CSS preprocessor only
quiz.explanation: The production picture includes CI/CD, load balancing in front of the app, and logging and monitoring once it is live.

exercise.prompt: Sketch a simple production path for a web app: developer commit → CI/CD → running instances behind a load balancer, plus one place logs or metrics would be sent. Label each box.
exercise.hint: A typical path is repo → build/test pipeline → deploy to several app servers, with a load balancer in front and a log or metrics store on the side.

lessons.content:
## From a laptop program to a production app

Once you know how one computer works, the next question is what a production-ready application looks like at a high level. Hayk walks through the path from code in a repository to a running service that can take traffic, store data, and recover when something breaks.

## Getting code to production: CI/CD

The first piece is a **CI/CD pipeline** — continuous integration and continuous deployment. The idea is that code goes from the repository through automated tests and pipeline checks and onto the production servers without someone copying files by hand. Common tools for this automation are Jenkins and GitHub Actions.

## Serving traffic and storing data

Once the app is in production, it has to handle many user requests. **Load balancers** and **reverse proxies** (Hayk mentions Nginx) spread those requests across multiple servers so the system stays usable during traffic spikes. The application also needs durable data, usually on an **external storage server** that is *not* on the same machine as the app. It is connected over the network. A production system often has several such services talking to one another, not a single process.

```text
Developers → repo → CI/CD (Jenkins / GitHub Actions)
                         ↓
Clients → load balancer / reverse proxy (e.g. Nginx)
                         ↓
              app servers  ──network──▶  storage
                         ↓
              logs, monitoring, alerts
```

## Logging, monitoring, and alerts

To know whether the system is healthy, you add **logging and monitoring**. It is standard to store logs on external services, outside the primary production server. On the backend, a process manager such as PM2 can help with logging and monitoring. On the frontend, a platform such as Sentry can capture and report errors in real time.

When logs or monitors show failing requests or other anomalies, an **alerting** service fires. Users might get a notification (from a generic “something went wrong” to a specific “payment failed”). A modern practice is to send those alerts into a tool the team already uses, such as a dedicated Slack channel, so someone can start investigating immediately.

## How teams actually debug

When an alert fires, developers should not debug on the live production system if they can avoid it. The usual sequence is:

1. Identify the issue, starting with the logs, looking for patterns or anomalies.
2. Recreate it in a **staging or test** environment. The golden rule is: never debug directly in production, so users are not affected by the investigation.
3. Use debugging tools against that safe copy of the app.
4. Ship a **hotfix** — a quick, temporary patch to restore service — and follow it later with a more permanent fix.

## Common pitfalls

- Deploying by hand with no pipeline, so tests are skipped and rollbacks are messy.
- Keeping the database on the same box as the app, so a machine failure takes both down.
- Debugging live in production and making a bad day worse.
- Having logs but no alerts, so no one looks until users complain.

## Key takeaways

- CI/CD (for example Jenkins or GitHub Actions) automates the path from repository to production.
- Load balancers and reverse proxies such as Nginx spread traffic; data usually lives on a separate storage server.
- Log and monitor on the backend (for example PM2) and frontend (for example Sentry), and alert into a place like Slack.
- Reproduce bugs in staging, not in production; use a hotfix to restore service, then a lasting fix.

lessons.title: CAP, throughput, latency, SLOs and SLAs

chapters.title: Design Requirements (CAP Theorem, Throughput, Latency, SLOs and SLAs)

lessons.summary: The section opens with what makes a good design: scalability as the system grows with its users, maintainability so future developers can change it, and efficiency in how resources are used, plus planning for failure. It then covers the CAP theorem (you can fully guarantee only two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance), throughput versus latency, and the difference between SLOs (internal targets) and SLAs (external commitments).

quiz.question: What does the CAP theorem say you can fully guarantee at once in a distributed system?
choices: Consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, always all three
Only two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Only throughput and latency
Only SLOs, never SLAs
quiz.explanation: When the network partitions, you usually have to trade between consistency and availability.

quiz.question: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
choices: They are two names for the same metric
Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how much work the system completes in a period
Throughput is only used for disks; latency is only used for networks
Latency measures availability; throughput measures consistency
quiz.explanation: A system can have high throughput and still feel slow to one user if latency is high.

quiz.question: How do SLOs and SLAs typically differ?
choices: SLOs are internal targets; SLAs are external commitments, often with consequences if missed
SLAs are only used by front-end teams; SLOs are only used by databases
An SLO is a legal contract; an SLA is a cache setting
They are identical terms
quiz.explanation: You set SLOs to run the service; an SLA is the promise you make to customers or partners.

exercise.prompt: Pick a system (for example a bank transfer API or a social feed). Write whether you would lean toward consistency or availability if the network partitions, and give one latency or throughput target you might set as an SLO.
exercise.hint: A bank usually favors consistency (correct balances) over always being available. A feed might accept slightly stale data to stay up. An SLO might be ‘p99 latency under 200 ms’ or ‘99.9% of requests succeed’.

lessons.content:
## What good design is aiming at

Before the tools and the theorems, Hayk frames what a *good* design actually means. He highlights three principles: **scalability** (the system can grow with its user base), **maintainability** (future developers can understand and improve it), and **efficiency** (you make good use of resources). Good design also means planning for failure: the system should not only work when everything is healthy, it should keep its composure when something breaks.

Underneath those principles, most systems do three kinds of work:

- **Moving data** — requests reaching servers, transfers between databases — optimized for speed and security.
- **Storing data** — not just “SQL or NoSQL,” but access patterns, indexing, and backups, so data is safe and available when needed.
- **Transforming data** — turning raw input into something useful, such as aggregating logs or converting a user-submitted value into another format.

Every design decision is a trade-off. A system tuned for reads may write slowly. A performance win may cost complexity. The goal is not a perfect architecture; it is the best fit for *this* use case, with honest compromises.

## The CAP theorem

The CAP theorem (Brewer’s theorem, after Eric Brewer) says that a distributed system can fully provide only two of these three properties at once:

| Letter | Meaning | Everyday picture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consistency | All nodes show the same data at the same time | An edit in a shared Google Doc appears for everyone immediately |
| Availability | The system keeps answering requests | An online store that is always open to take an order |
| Partition tolerance | The system keeps working when nodes cannot talk to each other | A group chat that continues even if one person drops off |

If you choose consistency and partition tolerance, you may have to give up some availability, and vice versa. A banking system, Hayk notes, often needs to be consistent and partition tolerant so financial records stay accurate, even if that means a transaction takes longer — a temporary hit to availability.

## Availability, SLOs, and SLAs

Availability is the question: is the system up when users need it? It is usually quoted as a percentage of uptime. “Five nines” is a common gold standard. The jumps between nines are huge: about **99.9%** availability allows roughly **8.76 hours** of downtime per year; two more nines (**99.999%**) is on the order of about **five minutes** a year. For a service where every second matters, that gap is the whole design problem.

Two related documents show up in real teams:

- **SLOs** (service level objectives) are internal goals. Example: “respond within 300 milliseconds, 99.9% of the time.”
- **SLAs** (service level agreements) are formal commitments to customers. If you promise 99.99% availability and miss it, the contract may require refunds or other compensation.

## Resilience: reliability, fault tolerance, redundancy

Building resilience means expecting the unexpected. That can mean redundant systems so a backup can take over, or a design that **degrades gracefully**: some features may fail, but the core still works.

Hayk separates three words that people blur together:

- **Reliability** — the system works correctly and consistently.
- **Fault tolerance** — how it behaves when something unexpected happens, including failures or attacks.
- **Redundancy** — having a spare ready if one part fails.

## Throughput versus latency

Speed has two different measurements, and optimizing one can hurt the other.

**Throughput** is how much work the system handles in a period of time:

- Server throughput in **requests per second (RPS)**
- Database throughput in **queries per second (QPS)**
- Data throughput in **bytes per second**

Higher RPS or QPS usually means more concurrent users can be served.

**Latency** is how long *one* request takes — the time from asking to getting an answer. A system can have high throughput and still feel slow if each request waits a long time, or low latency on a trickle of traffic that collapses when load rises. You need both numbers, and you need to know which one your users care about for the feature you are designing.

## Common pitfalls

- Treating CAP as “pick any two” without saying *in the presence of a partition* — partition tolerance is not optional on a real network, so the hard choice is often consistency versus availability.
- Quoting “five nines” without converting it into actual downtime.
- Confusing an SLO (a goal) with an SLA (a customer contract).
- Optimizing only throughput or only latency and calling the system “fast.”

## Key takeaways

- Good design balances scalability, maintainability, efficiency, and behavior under failure.
- Systems move, store, and transform data; every choice has trade-offs.
- CAP: a distributed system cannot simultaneously maximize consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
- Availability is measured in uptime; 99.9% and 99.999% imply very different downtime.
- SLOs are internal goals; SLAs are formal promises.
- Reliability, fault tolerance, and redundancy are related but not the same.
- Throughput is volume over time; latency is time per request.

lessons.title: TCP, UDP, DNS, and IP

chapters.title: Networking (TCP, UDP, DNS, IP Addresses & IP Headers)

lessons.summary: Networking basics cover how machines find each other and exchange packets. IP addresses identify hosts, and IP headers carry routing metadata. DNS maps human-readable names to addresses. TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable transport; UDP is a lighter, connectionless transport that does not guarantee delivery or order — a trade-off that shows up later in API and real-time protocol choices.

quiz.question: What is DNS used for?
choices: Compressing images before they are stored
Mapping a domain name to an IP address
Guaranteeing that UDP packets arrive in order
Encrypting a database at rest
quiz.explanation: DNS is the name system of the internet: example.com becomes an address a client can contact.

quiz.question: Which statement about TCP and UDP is accurate?
choices: UDP is always slower than TCP because it retries more often
TCP is connection-oriented and aims to deliver data reliably; UDP is lighter and does not guarantee delivery or order
TCP cannot be used for HTTP
UDP assigns IP addresses to hosts
quiz.explanation: TCP adds handshake, acknowledgements, and ordering. UDP skips that overhead.

exercise.prompt: For each of these, choose TCP or UDP and say why: a bank’s payment API, a live video call, and a DNS lookup (as typically designed).
exercise.hint: Payments usually want TCP’s reliability. Real-time media often uses UDP so a late packet can be dropped instead of stalling the stream. Classic DNS queries are often UDP.

lessons.content:
## How machines find and talk to each other

Networking is the set of rules and addresses that let computers exchange data. Hayk starts with the **IP address**, a unique identifier for a device on a network.

**IPv4** addresses are 32 bits, which allows on the order of 4 billion unique addresses — not enough for a world full of devices, which is why **IPv6** uses 128-bit addresses and a much larger space.

When two computers communicate, they send **packets**. Each packet has an IP header with information such as the sender’s and receiver’s addresses, so the data can be routed to the right place. That behavior is defined by the **Internet Protocol**. Above that, an application layer carries protocol-specific data, for example HTTP for the web, so the receiving application can interpret the payload correctly.

## TCP and UDP

At the transport layer, the two protocols you must be able to contrast are TCP and UDP.

**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) is built for reliable delivery. Hayk compares it to a delivery courier who not only arrives but checks that nothing is missing. Packets include a TCP header with port numbers and control flags. Reliability comes from features such as **sequence numbers**, which keep packets in order, and the **three-way handshake**, which sets up a connection before useful data flows. Use TCP when correctness and completeness matter more than raw speed.

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) is faster and less formal. It does not establish a connection first, and it does not guarantee delivery or order. That makes it a better fit for time-sensitive work such as video calls or live streaming, where a late packet is worse than a lost one, and some loss is acceptable.

| | TCP | UDP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection | Handshake first | No connection setup |
| Delivery | Reliable, ordered | Best effort, no order guarantee |
| Typical use | Web pages, email, most APIs | Live video, voice, some games |

## DNS

People type names, not raw IPs. **DNS** (the Domain Name System) is the internet’s phone book: it translates a domain name into an IP address. When you enter a URL, the browser sends a DNS query, gets an IP, and only then connects to the server.

ICANN coordinates global IP space and DNS. Registrars accredited by ICANN (Hayk mentions examples such as Namecheap) sell domain names to the public.

Common record types include:

- **A records** — map a name to an IPv4 address
- **AAAA records** — map a name to an IPv6 address

## Public vs private, static vs dynamic, firewalls and ports

A **public IP** is unique on the internet. A **private IP** is unique only inside a local network. An address can be **static** (permanently assigned) or **dynamic** (it changes over time). Dynamic addresses are common for residential connections.

Devices on a LAN can talk to each other directly. A **firewall** watches incoming and outgoing traffic and enforces what is allowed.

On a single machine, a **port** identifies a process or service. Combined with an IP address, it uniquely identifies a network service. Some ports are reserved by convention: **80** for HTTP, **22** for SSH, and so on.

```text
browser  --DNS A/AAAA-->  203.0.113.10:80  (public IP + HTTP port)
                 |
          firewall / LAN
                 |
         private IPs on local devices
```

## Common pitfalls

- Treating IPv4 as “enough addresses forever.”
- Using UDP for a bank transfer, or TCP for a live stream, without thinking about loss versus delay.
- Confusing a domain name with an IP; DNS is the translation step in between.
- Exposing a service on a well-known port with no firewall in front of it.

## Key takeaways

- IPv4 is 32-bit; IPv6 is 128-bit. Packets carry IP headers so they can be routed.
- TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless and faster, with possible loss.
- DNS maps names to IPs (A and AAAA records); ICANN and registrars run the naming ecosystem.
- Public vs private and static vs dynamic describe how addresses are assigned and who can reach them.
- Firewalls filter traffic; ports (such as 80 and 22) select a service on a host.

lessons.title: Application layer protocols

chapters.title: Application Layer Protocols (HTTP, WebSockets, WebRTC, MQTT, etc)

lessons.summary: Once packets can move, applications still need a protocol for meaning. HTTP is called out as the most common application-layer protocol, the request/response model for the web and many APIs. The lesson also covers WebSockets for an open bidirectional channel, WebRTC for real-time audio and video, MQTT for lightweight publish/subscribe (often used in IoT), and mentions protocols such as SSH in the same survey.

quiz.question: When would WebSockets usually be a better fit than plain request/response HTTP?
choices: For a one-off download of a static image
When the client and server need an open, bidirectional channel for frequent updates
When you only need to send a single form submission
When you want to avoid all networking
quiz.explanation: Chat, live feeds, and similar apps often need the server to push data without a new HTTP request each time.

quiz.question: Which protocol is commonly associated with lightweight publish/subscribe messaging, including IoT devices?
choices: FTP
MQTT
SMTP only
CSS
quiz.explanation: MQTT is designed as a compact pub/sub protocol for constrained clients and unreliable networks.

exercise.prompt: Choose a protocol (HTTP, WebSockets, WebRTC, or MQTT) for: (1) a product catalog API, (2) an in-browser video call, and (3) thousands of sensors reporting temperature. Write one reason for each.
exercise.hint: Catalog: HTTP. Video call: WebRTC. Sensors: MQTT (or a similar pub/sub protocol).

lessons.content:
## HTTP: a request/response conversation with no memory

The most common application-layer protocol is **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), built on TCP/IP. It is a request/response protocol, and Hayk asks you to picture a conversation with no memory: each interaction is separate. The server does not have to keep context between requests; each request carries what the server needs to understand it.

A request has **headers** (including the URL and method) and often a **body**. A response includes a **status code** that tells the client what happened:

| Range | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 2xx | Success — the request was received and processed |
| 3xx | Redirection — the client must take a further step |
| 4xx | Client error — bad syntax or a request the server cannot fulfill |
| 5xx | Server error — something went wrong on the server |

The common methods, and their usual intent, are:

- **GET** — fetch data
- **POST** — create data on the server
- **PUT** / **PATCH** — update a record
- **DELETE** — remove a record

HTTP as used for ordinary page loads is a one-way request/response cycle. That is enough for many apps, and too chatty for others.

## Real-time and other common protocols

For live updates, **WebSockets** provide a two-way channel over a single long-lived connection, so the server can push data without a new HTTP round trip each time. Typical uses are chat, live sports scores, and stock feeds — anything where the “conversation” should stay open.

Email uses a small family of protocols:

- **SMTP** — sending messages between servers (and what most clients use to send)
- **IMAP** — retrieve and manipulate mail on the server, which suits people who read email on several devices
- **POP3** — download mail to a local client, typically when mail is managed on one device

File and remote-access protocols include **FTP**, still used for site maintenance and large transfers, and **SSH** (Secure Shell), used to log into a remote machine, run commands, and transfer files securely over an untrusted network.

For real-time media in the browser, **WebRTC** supports voice, video, and file sharing between browsers without extra plugins — the basis of many video calls and live streams.

Messaging and IoT have their own tools: **MQTT** is a lightweight messaging protocol for devices with little CPU and low bandwidth; **AMQP** is a more robust, enterprise-oriented messaging protocol (used, for example, by RabbitMQ).

## RPC

**RPC** (remote procedure call) lets a program on one computer invoke a function that actually runs on another, as if the call were local. The network details are abstracted away. Many application protocols use RPC underneath: an HTTP request might trigger an RPC on a backend; an SMTP server might use RPC internally to process mail or talk to a database.

You do not need to memorize every protocol on the internet. Hayk’s point is that these are the ones you will meet constantly in web and backend work, and you should know what problem each one is for.

## Common pitfalls

- Treating HTTP as if the server remembered the last request (it does not, unless you add cookies, tokens, or some other state).
- Using GET to change data.
- Choosing POP3 for someone who needs the same mailbox on a phone and a laptop; IMAP is the better default there.
- Reaching for HTTP polling when a WebSocket (or similar) would avoid a storm of request/response cycles.

## Key takeaways

- HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol with methods, headers, bodies, and 2xx–5xx status codes.
- GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, and DELETE map onto typical read/create/update/delete operations.
- WebSockets keep a two-way connection for real-time updates.
- SMTP sends email; IMAP and POP3 receive it in different styles.
- FTP and SSH handle files and remote login; WebRTC, MQTT, and AMQP cover media, IoT, and enterprise messaging.
- RPC makes a remote call look like a local function.

modules.title: APIs, caches, proxies, and load balancers

lessons.title: API design
lessons.summary: This section starts from API basics and works toward practical habits for interfaces that other developers can use as a system grows: clear resource-oriented contracts, consistent naming and status codes, versioning so you can change a contract safely, and thinking about pagination, errors, and idempotency so retries do not corrupt data.

quiz.question: Why does API versioning matter in a production system?
choices: It lets you change a contract without immediately breaking existing clients
It makes DNS resolve faster
It replaces the need for authentication
It automatically shards your database
quiz.explanation: A versioned path or header gives old clients a stable API while new clients adopt the new one.

quiz.question: What does it mean for an API operation to be idempotent?
choices: It can never return an error
Repeating the same request has the same effect as doing it once
It must use UDP
It always creates a new record
quiz.explanation: Idempotency is important when networks retry. A well-designed PUT or a request with an idempotency key should not double-charge or double-create.

exercise.prompt: Design a tiny REST-style API for a library: list endpoints to list books, get one book, and borrow a book. Note one status code you would return on success and one on a client error, and say whether borrow should be idempotent if the client retries.
exercise.hint: Example: GET /books, GET /books/{id}, POST /books/{id}/borrow. 200 or 201 on success, 400 or 404 on client errors. Retries should not borrow the same copy twice.

lessons.content:
## Start with the operations and the contract

API design is about the contract between clients and a service: what goes in, and what comes out. Hayk uses an e-commerce example in the spirit of a platform like Shopify. A seller provides product details (input); a query returns product information (output). Most of that contract is about how **CRUD** operations — create, read, update, delete — are exposed.

A typical REST-shaped layout looks like this:

- `POST /api/products` — create, with details in the body
- `GET /api/products` — list
- `GET /api/products/{id}` — read one
- `PUT` or `PATCH /api/products/{id}` — update
- `DELETE /api/products/{id}` — remove

Relationships show up in the path too. To fetch one user’s orders you might use `GET /users/{userId}/orders`. Common query parameters include `limit` and `offset` for pagination, or a start and end date to filter — so a client can ask for a slice of data instead of everything at once.

You also choose a **communication protocol** (HTTP, WebSockets, and others) and a **data format** (JSON, XML, or Protocol Buffers). Those choices usually come with a *paradigm*: REST, GraphQL, or gRPC.

## REST, GraphQL, and gRPC

**REST** (Representational State Transfer) is stateless: each request must carry everything the server needs. It uses standard HTTP methods and is easy for browsers and mobile apps to consume. Data is usually JSON. The downside is **over-fetching** or **under-fetching**: a fixed endpoint may return too many fields, or not enough, so you add more endpoints to cover special cases.

**GraphQL** lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs, which avoids that over- and under-fetching. Queries are strongly typed. The costs: a heavy query can hurt the server, requests are typically sent as POST, and the HTTP status is often **200 even when there are errors**, with the error details inside the body — so clients must read the payload, not only the status code.

**gRPC** (gRPC Remote Procedure Calls) runs on **HTTP/2**, which brings features such as multiplexing and server push. It serializes data with **Protocol Buffers**, which is compact and efficient — a good fit for service-to-service traffic in a microservice system. The downside is that payloads are less human-readable than JSON, and you need HTTP/2 support.

| Style | Strength | Watch-outs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| REST | Simple, standard HTTP, easy clients | Over/under-fetching, extra endpoints |
| GraphQL | Client specifies the exact shape | Query cost, errors often hidden behind HTTP 200 |
| gRPC | Efficient, HTTP/2, great between services | Less readable, needs HTTP/2 |

## Idempotent reads and mutations

A well-designed **GET** should be **idempotent**: calling it many times does not change server data, and it should return the same result if the data has not changed. GET must not mutate data. If you need to create or update, use POST or PUT (or PATCH). That rule keeps caches, retries, and client code honest.

## Common pitfalls

- Nesting URLs arbitrarily without thinking about the relationship you are expressing.
- Returning an entire catalog when the client needed one page; add pagination and filters.
- Treating a GraphQL HTTP 200 as “success” without checking the error list in the body.
- Using GET to delete or update, which surprises caches and any client that retries.

## Key takeaways

- Design the CRUD contract first: paths, methods, inputs, and outputs, as in a product API.
- Model relationships in the URL, and support pagination and filtering on list endpoints.
- REST is stateless HTTP; GraphQL lets clients shape the response; gRPC plus protobufs is efficient over HTTP/2.
- GET should be safe and idempotent; mutations belong on POST, PUT, or PATCH.

lessons.title: Caching and CDNs
lessons.summary: Hayk motivates caching with a company hosting a website on a cloud server that is far from some users. A cache stores a computed or fetched result closer to the next reader, and a CDN is a geographically distributed cache so users hit a nearby edge instead of the origin. You also have to plan invalidation and what happens on a cache miss, because stale or missing data is the usual trade-off. Faster load times are treated as part of a better user experience.

quiz.question: What problem do caches and CDNs mainly try to improve?
choices: They replace the need for a database
They reduce latency and load on the origin by serving stored copies of data or content
They guarantee strong consistency across every region
They make CAP trade-offs disappear
quiz.explanation: A cache hit avoids a slower trip to the origin. A CDN does that from a location nearer the user.

quiz.question: What is a cache invalidation problem?
choices: Deciding when a stored copy is too old or must be replaced after the source changes
Converting HTTP to WebSockets
Assigning IP addresses to cache servers
Writing the first line of a unit test
quiz.explanation: If you never invalidate, users can see stale data. If you invalidate too aggressively, you lose the benefit of the cache.

exercise.prompt: For a news website’s article pages, say what you might cache at a CDN, what should probably not be cached for long, and one way you would expire or purge a page after an editor updates it.
exercise.hint: The rendered article and images are good CDN candidates. Personalized account widgets should stay short-lived or uncached. Use a short TTL, a cache key with a version, or a purge when the article is published.

lessons.content:
## Why distance hurts, and what caching does

Hayk starts with a concrete latency problem. A site hosted in a Google Cloud data center in Finland might load in around 100 milliseconds for users in Europe, but take 3 to 5 seconds for users in Mexico. Caching and content delivery networks (CDNs) exist to cut that kind of delay.

**Caching** stores a copy of data in a faster, temporary place so later requests can be served without repeating expensive work. When the copy is found, that is a **cache hit**. When it is not, that is a **cache miss**, and the system must fetch from the origin. The **hit ratio** is the share of requests served from the cache; a higher ratio means the cache is doing its job. You can often see a hit or miss in a header such as `X-Cache`.

## Browser caching

The first common place to cache is the **browser**. The browser stores site resources — typically HTML, CSS, and JavaScript bundles — in a directory on the user’s machine. On a later visit it can load those files locally instead of downloading everything again.

Developers control this with the `Cache-Control` header. An example in the lesson sets it to 7,200 seconds, which is two hours. Users can disable caching in browser settings, and developers can disable it from dev tools (in Chrome, a “Disable cache” option on the Network tab) so they always see fresh files while debugging.

## Server-side caching and write policies

**Server caching** stores frequently used data near the application, so you avoid repeated heavy work such as database queries. The cache may live in the application server’s memory, on disk, or on a separate cache server. **Redis** is a common in-memory choice.

The usual read path is: check the cache first; on a hit, return that data; on a miss, query the database, return the result, and store it in the cache for next time.

Writes have several policies, and they trade speed for safety:

| Policy | What happens on write | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Write-around | Write goes to permanent storage and skips the cache | Simpler when write speed is less critical |
| Write-through | Write goes to the cache and to storage at the same time | Stronger consistency, often slower writes |
| Write-back (write-behind) | Write goes to the cache first, storage is updated later | Faster writes, but a crash can lose data not yet flushed |

When the cache is full, an **eviction policy** decides what to drop. Two common rules are **least recently used (LRU)** and **first in, first out (FIFO)**.

## Content delivery networks

A **CDN** is a geographically distributed set of caches. Instead of every user in Mexico hitting Finland, they can be served from a nearby edge location that already has a copy of the static (and sometimes dynamic) content. That is the practical answer to the 3-to-5-second load time in the opening example: move popular bytes closer to the reader.

```text
User in Mexico  →  nearby CDN edge (hit: fast)
                →  origin in Finland (miss: slower, then cached at the edge)
```

## Common pitfalls

- Caching something that changes often without a short TTL, so users see stale data.
- Using write-back for data you cannot afford to lose.
- Debugging with a warm browser cache and thinking the server is broken.
- Treating “add a CDN” as a fix for a slow *dynamic* query that was never cacheable.

## Key takeaways

- Caches store copies so future requests are faster; measure hits, misses, and hit ratio.
- Browsers cache static assets under `Cache-Control`; server caches (for example Redis) sit in front of databases.
- Write-around, write-through, and write-back make different consistency versus speed trade-offs.
- LRU and FIFO are typical eviction policies when the cache is full.
- CDNs reduce geographic latency by serving from nearby edges.

lessons.title: Forward and reverse proxies
lessons.summary: Proxy servers act as an intermediary on the request path. A forward proxy sits in front of clients and can send their requests onward (for example for egress control or filtering). A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers: clients talk to the proxy, and it forwards to the right origin. Reverse proxies are often used for TLS termination, caching, routing, and shielding backends.

quiz.question: Where does a reverse proxy sit?
choices: In front of your servers, so clients send requests to the proxy rather than directly to each origin
Only on the user’s laptop, never in the data center
Between two database replicas only
Inside the CPU cache
quiz.explanation: Clients know the proxy’s address. The proxy chooses or protects the backend.

quiz.question: What is a typical job of a forward proxy?
choices: Sharding a database by user id
Acting on behalf of clients when they make outbound requests, for example to filter or control egress
Writing CI/CD pipelines
Replacing DNS entirely
quiz.explanation: Forward proxies represent the client side; reverse proxies represent the server side.

exercise.prompt: Draw or describe two tiny diagrams: a browser going through a forward proxy to the public internet, and many browsers going to a reverse proxy that forwards to three app servers. Label which proxy is which.
exercise.hint: Forward: clients → forward proxy → internet. Reverse: clients → reverse proxy → your app servers.

lessons.content:
## A proxy is an intermediary

A **proxy** sits between a client that wants a resource and a server that provides it. It receives the client’s request, forwards it (or blocks or changes it), and returns the server’s response. People use proxies for caching, anonymizing requests, controlling access, and spreading load.

Hayk lists several types, then spends the most time on the two you must be able to draw: forward and reverse.

Other types, in brief:

- **Open proxy** — anyone can connect; often used to anonymize browsing or bypass restrictions.
- **Transparent proxy** — visible to the client, does not hide that a proxy is there; often used for caching and filtering.
- **Anonymous proxy** — identifiable as a proxy, but it does not hand the client’s real IP to the destination.
- **Distorting proxy** — like an anonymous proxy, but it sends a *wrong* original IP on purpose.
- **High-anonymity (elite) proxy** — hard to detect; it does not send headers such as `X-Forwarded-For`.

## Forward proxies

A **forward proxy** sits in front of *clients*, usually on an internal network, and sends their requests out to the internet. The client talks to the proxy first. The proxy applies rules: allow, modify, or block. When it forwards the request, the target server often sees the **proxy’s IP**, not the client’s.

Typical uses:

- Controlling and monitoring employee web use, blocking unrelated sites, and scanning incoming content for malware.
- Caching popular sites to save bandwidth on a constrained network.
- Anonymizing browsing so websites cannot easily see the client’s IP.
- A more specific example Hayk gives is “Instagram proxies”: marketers use forward proxies to appear as different locations or users so they can manage multiple accounts or collect data without being flagged as quickly.

```text
Client  →  forward proxy  →  internet servers
           (hides or controls the client)
```

## Reverse proxies

A **reverse proxy** sits in front of *one or more web servers* and intercepts requests from the internet. Clients talk only to the proxy and may never learn how many servers sit behind it — the proxy hides the servers’ identity the way a forward proxy hides the client’s.

Common jobs for a reverse proxy:

- **Load balancing** — spread requests so no one server is overwhelmed.
- **Web acceleration** — including compressing inbound and outbound traffic, and offloading work such as TLS/SSL so app servers can focus on the application.
- **Security** — a single front door you can harden.

```text
Internet clients  →  reverse proxy  →  server A
                                  →  server B
                     (hides and protects the servers)
```

If you remember only one contrast: a forward proxy stands in front of clients; a reverse proxy stands in front of servers.

## Common pitfalls

- Drawing a “proxy” on a diagram without saying which side it sits on.
- Assuming every proxy anonymizes the client; a reverse proxy is not for that.
- Forgetting that a reverse proxy can also cache, terminate TLS, and compress, not only balance load.

## Key takeaways

- A proxy is a middle box that can cache, filter, anonymize, or balance traffic.
- Forward proxies sit in front of clients and often hide the client IP; used for control, caching, and privacy.
- Reverse proxies sit in front of servers, hide those servers, and often load-balance, accelerate, and protect them.
- Open, transparent, anonymous, distorting, and elite proxies describe how visible the client and the proxy are.

lessons.title: Load balancers
lessons.summary: Load balancers are described as perhaps the most popular use of proxy servers. They distribute incoming traffic across multiple instances so no single server is the only path, which improves availability and helps you scale horizontally. They often run health checks and stop sending traffic to sick nodes. A load balancer can itself become a single point of failure if you only run one.

quiz.question: What is the main job of a load balancer?
choices: Compile frontend assets
Distribute incoming traffic across multiple backends and usually avoid unhealthy ones
Convert SQL queries into NoSQL documents
Issue TLS certificates only
quiz.explanation: It spreads load and, with health checks, can take failing instances out of rotation.

quiz.question: Why can a single load balancer still be a problem?
choices: Because load balancers cannot use TCP
Because it can become a single point of failure if it is the only entry point and it goes down
Because it prevents you from using DNS
Because it makes caching illegal
quiz.explanation: Production setups often use more than one load balancer, or a managed service with redundancy.

exercise.prompt: List two load-balancing algorithms and one situation where you would pick each. Then add a note about what a health check should do if an instance starts returning 500s.
exercise.hint: Round robin is simple when instances are similar. Least connections can help if some requests are long-lived. A health check should take the failing instance out of the pool until it recovers.

lessons.content:
## Spreading traffic on purpose

Load balancers are one of the most common uses of a proxy. They distribute incoming requests across a pool of servers so no single machine takes all the load. That raises both the capacity and the reliability of the application.

## Algorithms

Hayk walks through the usual strategies. You should be able to pick one and say why it fits.

| Algorithm | How a server is chosen | Good when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Round robin | Next server in a rotating list, then back to the first | Servers are similar and work is even |
| Least connections | The server with the fewest open connections | Tasks are long, or load is uneven |
| Least response time | Lowest response time and few connections | You want the fastest reply |
| IP hashing | A hash of the client IP maps to a server | The same client should keep hitting the same server (session persistence) |
| Weighted round robin / weighted least connections | Stronger servers get a higher weight and more work | Machines in the pool have different CPU or RAM |
| Geographic | The closest (or region-required) server | A global service where latency matters |
| Consistent hashing | Clients and nodes are placed on a hash ring | You want stable assignment as nodes are added or removed |

**Consistent hashing** is worth an extra picture: the hash space is a circle (a ring). Both nodes and keys are hashed onto that ring. A key belongs to the next node around the ring. When a node is added or removed, only nearby keys move, instead of reshuffling the whole pool. It also helps the same client keep finding the same server.

## Health checks, products, and failure

A load balancer should **health-check** its servers continuously and send traffic only to instances that are up. If a server fails, the balancer stops using it until it recovers.

Load balancers come as hardware, software, cloud services, or virtual appliances. Examples from the lesson:

- Hardware: F5 BIG-IP (local traffic management, global server load balancing, security); Citrix (formerly NetScaler) for load balancing, content switching, and acceleration.
- Software: HAProxy (TCP and HTTP); Nginx (often a web server, also a load balancer and reverse proxy).
- Cloud: AWS Elastic Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer, Google Cloud Load Balancing.
- Virtual / software-defined: examples such as VMware’s application delivery controller, deployable on-premises or in the cloud.

A *single* load balancer is itself a **single point of failure**. If it dies, clients may be unable to reach any of the healthy app servers behind it. The usual mitigation is **redundancy**: run more than one load balancer, often as a pair, so a standby can take over if the active one fails.

```text
Clients → LB pair (active / standby)
              ↓          ↓
           server 1   server 2   (health-checked)
```

## Common pitfalls

- Using plain round robin when sessions must stick to one server; consider IP hashing or consistent hashing.
- Ignoring server size differences; use weights.
- Forgetting health checks, so traffic keeps going to a dead instance.
- Putting one load balancer in front of everything and calling the system highly available.

## Key takeaways

- Load balancers spread requests to raise capacity and reliability.
- Choose an algorithm to match evenness, session stickiness, geography, or mixed hardware.
- Health checks should remove bad servers from the pool automatically.
- Hardware, software, and cloud products all exist; Nginx and HAProxy are common software options.
- Redundant balancers avoid a single point of failure.

lessons.title: Sharding, replication, ACID, and scaling

chapters.title: Databases (Sharding, Replication, ACID, Vertical & Horizontal Scaling)

lessons.summary: The course treats a database deep-dive as essential for system design interviews. Vertical scaling means a bigger machine; horizontal scaling means more machines. Replication copies data to other nodes for reads, backups, or failover. Sharding splits data across nodes so each holds only a part of the set. ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) describes the guarantees people expect from a transactional database, each with trade-offs in complexity, consistency, and cost.

quiz.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling for a database?
choices: Vertical means a larger machine; horizontal means adding more machines
Vertical means more regions only; horizontal means faster disks only
They are two words for sharding
Horizontal scaling never requires application changes
quiz.explanation: Vertical scaling is simpler until you hit the limits of one box. Horizontal scaling adds capacity by distributing work.

quiz.question: What does sharding do?
choices: It encrypts every query
It splits data across multiple nodes so each one stores only a subset
It always makes every replica identical and writable
It replaces the need for backups
quiz.explanation: A shard key decides which node owns a row or document. That is different from replication, which copies the same data.

quiz.question: What do the letters in ACID stand for?
choices: Availability, Caching, Indexing, Deployment
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Auth, Compression, I/O, Disk
Append, Copy, Import, Delete
quiz.explanation: Those four properties describe a traditional transactional store: a unit of work either completes fully, leaves valid state, does not interfere badly with others, and survives a crash once committed.

exercise.prompt: You have a users table that no longer fits on one machine. In a short paragraph, say whether you would first try vertical scaling, read replicas, or sharding, and what trade-off your first choice accepts.
exercise.hint: A common path is: bigger machine first (simple, finite), then read replicas if the bottleneck is reads (writes still hit the primary), then sharding when a single primary cannot hold or write the data (more operational complexity).

lessons.content:
## Picking a store for your data

The last concept lesson is about databases: what kinds exist, how you scale them, and how you make access faster.

**Relational (SQL)** databases organize data in tables with a fixed schema and, typically, foreign keys that relate rows. They are a strong fit when relationships and strict structure matter.

**NoSQL** databases are a family, not one product. Hayk mentions MongoDB, Cassandra, and Redis as popular examples, and three shapes:

- Key-value, such as Redis
- Document, such as MongoDB
- Graph, such as Neo4j

NoSQL systems are often described as schema-less and without the same foreign-key style of linking. They can be a better fit for unstructured data, fast iteration, simple queries, and horizontal scale.

**In-memory** databases keep data in RAM for very fast reads and writes. Redis and Memcached are the usual examples. They are used heavily for caching and session storage. Hayk compares them to a whiteboard: great for quick work, not the same thing as durable disk storage.

## Scaling: vertical, sharding, and replication

**Vertical scaling** (scale up) means giving one database machine more CPU, RAM, faster disks, or a better network. It is straightforward, and it hits a hard ceiling: one box can only grow so far.

**Horizontal scaling** (scale out) means adding machines and spreading data. Two main techniques are sharding and replication.

**Sharding** splits the dataset into pieces (shards) on different servers. Strategies include:

- **Range-based** — a key’s range decides the shard
- **Directory-based** — a lookup service tells you which database holds the row
- **Geographic** — data is split by region

**Replication** keeps copies on several servers for availability. In **master–slave** (primary–replica) replication, one primary takes writes and replicas are typically read-only. In **master–master** (multi-primary) replication, more than one node can accept reads and writes.

```text
                    ┌─ replica (reads)
primary (writes) ───┼─ replica (reads)
                    └─ replica (reads)
```

## Faster access: cache and indexes

Scaling is one problem; **speed of access** is another. Two techniques appear here:

- **Caching**, including database-side caching with an in-memory store such as Redis, so frequent queries are not re-run every time.
- **Indexing**, which helps the database find rows without scanning an entire table. Indexes make reads faster; they also add write cost and storage, so you index the access paths you actually use.

Together with the earlier lessons on CAP, latency, and throughput, this is the vocabulary for talking about “where does the data live, and how do we grow?” in a design interview.

## Common pitfalls

- Scaling up only, then discovering the machine class has a maximum.
- Sharding on a key that looks even at first and then becomes a hotspot (for example, sharding by a low-cardinality country field).
- Using a multi-primary setup without a plan for write conflicts.
- Treating Redis as the only copy of data you cannot afford to lose.

## Key takeaways

- SQL databases are structured and relational; NoSQL covers key-value, document, and graph styles; in-memory stores such as Redis and Memcached are built for speed.
- Vertical scaling upgrades one machine; horizontal scaling adds machines.
- Sharding splits data (range, directory, or geography); replication copies it (primary–replica or multi-primary).
- Caches and indexes are the usual ways to make repeated access faster.
